The earliest observations of spectroscopic phenomena can be traced back to experiments conducted by Isaac Newton in the late 17th century. He demonstrated that white light could be separated into its component colors using a prism, revealing the spectrum of visible light.

In the early 19th century, Joseph von Fraunhofer made significant contributions to spectroscopy by systematically studying the absorption lines in the solar spectrum. He also discovered hundreds of dark lines, known as

, which are caused by the absorption of specific wavelengths of light by elements in the Sun's atmosphere. Gustav Kirchhoff and Robert Bunsen further advanced the field of spectroscopy in the mid-19th century. They developed the technique of

, which involves heating samples in a flame to produce characteristic emission spectra. Their work laid the foundation for quantitative analysis of chemical elements based on their spectral signatures.

The development of quantum mechanics in the early 20th century revolutionized our understanding of atomic structure and spectral lines. Scientists such as Niels Bohr, Max Planck, and Werner Heisenberg formulated theories to explain the discrete energy levels of atoms and the quantized nature of electromagnetic radiation. The Bohr model of the atom, proposed by Niels Bohr in 1913, provided a theoretical framework for understanding atomic spectra and the transitions of electrons between energy levels.
Throughout the 20th and 21st centuries, spectroscopic techniques have continued to evolve with technological advancements and instrumentation. Developing techniques such as

has expanded the range of applications in fields such as chemistry, physics, biology, materials science, and medicine. Innovations in detectors, lasers, optics, and computational methods have enabled researchers to achieve higher sensitivity, resolution, and versatility in spectroscopic measurements.

- Spectral imaging combines spectroscopy and imaging, generating a 3‑D spectral data cube I(
- The data cube contains two spatial dimensions (
Optical path: Scanning mirror moves across scene, one spatial point at a time. Each single point acquires its complete full spectrum. Build cube by scanning every pixel point‑by‑point.
✅ Pros: High spectral quality for each sampled point; good SNR.
❌ Cons: Two‑axis mechanical scanning; long acquisition time; moving‑part artifacts.

Optical path: Simultaneously captures an entire line of spatial information plus full spectrum for each pixel on that line. Complete 2‑D spatial area is obtained via relative platform motion (aircraft / satellite / translation stage).
✅ Pros: Much faster than whiskbroom; widely used in remote sensing.
❌ Cons: Depends on steady relative movement between sensor and target.

Optical path: Keep the whole scene stationary on detector; use tunable optical filters (AOTF, LCTF, FPI, LVF) to sequentially select one wavelength band. Stack series of 2‑D images to reconstruct the full 3‑D data cube.
✅ Pros: Captures full‑field scene for each wavelength; no spatial mechanical scanning.
❌ Cons: Wavelength scanning takes time; poor performance for dynamic moving scenes.
Trade‑off Between Spatial Resolution and Spectral Resolution
- In conventional spectral‑imaging optical systems, there exists an intrinsic trade‑off between spatial resolution and spectral resolution [1].
- Higher spectral resolution requires more, narrower spectral bands. Under limited photon budget and detector constraints, this often sacrifices spatial sampling performance.
- If you pursue fine spatial details (high spatial resolution), the number of available spectral channels will be limited.

- Advanced approaches such as snapshot imaging and compressive computational imaging can mitigate this conflict, but cannot completely eliminate the fundamental physical limits from photon availability.

The pros of using Hyperspectral Imaging in different applications such as agriculture, and food quality estimation are as follows [2]:
(i) It is a non-invasive, non-contact, non-destructive technology that ensures the quality and safety of food goods.
(ii) The experiments use no chemicals therefore environmentally safe.
(iii) The time required to process for quality evaluation and food control/storage is low compared to chemical and traditional approaches.
(iv) It gives an improved understanding of the chemical elements of food products and is generally known as chemical imaging.
(v) It provides appropriate area selection for critical analysis of the image.

(vi) It gains spatial and spectral information together to provide more appropriate and accurate data concerning chemical samples from interested platforms and enhance a chance to data refine and achieve further experiments.
Despite its pros, Hyperspectral Imaging also has some cons [
(i) A hyperspectral imaging system is highly costly compared to other image processing techniques.
(ii) Since the data size of hyperspectral imaging is large, there is a demand for high-speed computers for the processing of data and extensive capacity drives for the storage of data.
(iii) While acquiring the images, the signal could be impacted by ambient surroundings such as scattering, illumination, etc. therefore producing a destitute signal-to-noise ratio.
(iv) Detection and identification of different items within the equivalent image using spectral data is mostly difficult except the diverse objects have distinct absorption features.
